newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: World tea prices seen firm on crop shortfall.
newsitem.headline: World tea prices seen firm on crop shortfall.

text.p: Consumers across the world are likely to pay higher prices for tea this year as production levels have dropped sharply in main exporting countries while demand has remained stable, industry officials said.
They said dry weather in Kenya and Sri Lanka, the two main exporters, has pushed global production of tea down after reaching record levels in 1996.
The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) forecast in a report on Tuesday that world tea prices will rise in the near future on falling output.
"Since global output for 1997 is expected to be lower and demand likely to remain stable, consumers will face higher world tea prices," the FAO said.
The Rome-based FAO said tea production rose three percent year-on-year in 1996 to a record 2,691,000 tonnes.
"There is an overall shortage of around 35 million kg in the global market," said V. Ramaswamy, director of Carritt Moran & Company, a leading tea auctioneer in India.

The FAO said dry weather in Africa and Sri Lanka was to blame for a fall in global production in the first half of the year. Kenya was particularly badly hit, with 1997 first quarter production down 37 percent year-on-year.
April and May have not brought respite for Kenya either, Mombasa-based Africa Tea Brokers (ATB) said.
They said tea production in Kenya in the first five months was nearly 45 percent lower at 80.47 million kg against 116.43 million in the same period last year.

"In all tea growing areas temperatures have been low with some rainfall. Hailstorms have also been reported. After the post-drought flush, growth has been inhibited with banjhi in evidence and crops are low. Leaf intake has dropped," ATB said.
The situation in other African tea producing countries was no better. Malawi, Tanzania and Zimbabwe had all shown a drop in tea production in the first quarter, ATB said.

Sri Lanka, which produced a record harvest of 258.4 million kg in 1996, had a 7.2 million kg deficit up to April this year, producing 76 million kg against 83.3 million in the same period of 1996, brokers John Keells said in a report.
But brokers said on Thursday that production had risen in May and June and predicted Sri Lanka would end the year at around 254 million kg.

"Production in May was 27.4 million kg against 25.6 million in the same month last year. June also looks fairly good and we are expecting around 23-24 million kg against 19.8 million last year," said Sudath Munasinghe of brokers John Keells.
Prices at this week's Colombo auction were slightly down, mainly on higher availability and lower quality, after touching record highs in past weeks.
But Munasinghe said overall price levels were seen higher this year since Kenya was badly off and India was only marginally up in the first four months.
Tea officials said India's tea exports in 1997 were expected to be same as last year despite an anticipated fall in domestic output as global supplies were low amid a huge surge in demand.
"Exports will be the same as last year despite an anticipated fall in the crop as there is an increased demand from Russia, Poland and Germany," Ramaswamy said.
India exported 154 million kg of tea last year. Industry officials expect tea production in 1997 to fall to 760 million kg from 780 million kg last year.
It produced about 54 million kg of tea between January and March, down by 4.7 million kg in the same period last year.

Bangladesh output was down too. Drought in the early months and a cyclone in coastal Chittagong in May had affected production, brokers there said. They said production was not likely to top last year's 55.13 million kg and may well be below the 54 million kg achieved in 1995.
Traders said prices had risen sharply at Chittagong auctions and the trend was likely to continue.
